title: A hard ending, read as allegory
hookLine: the goldsmith she loves is brought and poisoned; Rumi reads it as a parable of false loves, and literal readers rightly flinch

lines: STORIES THAT MAKE YOU SAY, WAIT.
cards: Old books have stories that are hard to read, where something happens that makes a modern reader put the book down and say, wait, what? You can pretend the passage isn't there. You can throw out the whole book.

Or you can do the harder thing: read it closely, notice what the author was doing, and still say honestly, this troubles me. The story of the king and the handmaid ends in a way that can stop a modern reader cold.
I'm not going to skip it. Today, a hard ending.

teach.h: THE GOLDSMITH IS LURED WITH GOLD.
teach.b: The physician tells the king: send for the goldsmith in Samarkand, and tempt him with gold and fine robes. The goldsmith comes, proud and delighted, leaving his home and family. The king gives him the girl in marriage.
For six months they're happy, and she gets well. Then the physician gives the goldsmith a drink that makes him sicken.

teach.h: HE FADES, AND HER LOVE FADES.
teach.b: His good looks fade, and as his beauty goes, her love goes with it. And he dies. Near the end he says, in effect, my beauty killed me, the way a deer is hunted for its musk.
It's grim, and Rumi knows it.
He steps in: this was not done out of lust or greed; the physician acted on God's command.
He compares it to a story in the Quran, where a mysterious servant of God, whom tradition calls Khidr, kills a boy, and Moses is horrified until he's shown a hidden reason.
Sufi commentators have read the whole story as allegory. The king is the spirit, the girl is the soul, and the goldsmith is a love for surfaces, for things that look golden and fade.
The physician is the guide who lets that false love run its course until the soul sees through it. In that reading, nobody real is poisoned; an illusion dies.
Readers who take it as a story about people rightly flinch: an innocent man is lured from home and killed. Both reactions are honest, and this path doesn't smooth that over.
You can learn from what Rumi meant and still say plainly: this is hard to read.

how: Commentators on the Masnavi, from medieval Sufi scholars to modern teachers, have read the end of the king and the handmaid as an allegory of the soul freed from a false love, and some modern readers also name how troubling it is taken literally.

games.q: who is who, in the allegory — tap the pairs.

s: Rumi hides the killing and hopes you won't notice
he steps in himself, says it was done at God's command, and compares it to a Quran story.
Rumi compares the physician to the servant of God in the Quran who kills a boy
tradition names that servant Khidr; Moses is horrified until he's shown the hidden reason.
there's only one acceptable way to read the ending
Sufi commentators read it as allegory; literal readers flinch. both reactions are honest.

games.q: you're reading an old story you love, and the ending troubles you. what do you do?
o: skip the passage and keep the rest.
read it closely, learn what the author meant, and say honestly it troubles you.
games.why: this path does the third: Rumi's allegory of false love, told fully, and the honest flinch named too.

practice: Bring to mind a story you grew up with, from a scripture, a family legend, a movie or a fairy tale, that looks different depending on how you read it. Hold the first reading, then the second, without choosing between them yet.
Notice what it's like to keep both in your hands, the meaning and the discomfort; that's part of reading old books well.

wordCard.voice: Khidr, the mysterious servant of God in the Quran whose hidden reasons parallel the physician's hard choice. Today's word.
